theme: Manasseh’s repentance; Josiah; exile; Cyrus’s decree
readingInstruction: Read 2 Chronicles 33:1-36:23. Manasseh sins, repents, and is restored. Josiah finds the Book of the Law. Then the kings fall one by one, and the temple is burned. The book ends with a decree of Cyrus. Read the final verses twice.
settingTheScene: The last four chapters of Chronicles trace the fall of Judah. Manasseh is the worst king, and the Chronicler tells a story found nowhere else: his repentance in Babylon. Josiah’s reform is the last great revival. Then come four weak kings, the siege, and the exile. The book closes not with defeat but with an invitation: “Let him go up.” It ends where Ezra begins.
observation: “Manasseh led Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem astray, to do more evil than the nations” (33:9).
“And when he was in distress, he entreated the favor of the LORD his God and humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers” (33:12).
“Then Manasseh knew that the LORD was God” (33:13).
“And Josiah… while he was still a boy, began to seek the God of David his father” (34:3).
“Hilkiah the priest found the Book of the Law of the LORD given through Moses” (34:14).
“Because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before God” (34:27).
“But they kept mocking the messengers of God, despising his words and scoffing at his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD rose against his people, until there was no remedy” (36:16).
“Whoever is among you of all his people, may the LORD his God be with him. Let him go up” (36:23).
interpretation:
Manasseh reigned for 55 years, the longest of any king. He rebuilt high places, set up altars to Baal in the temple, practiced sorcery, and sacrificed his sons. He led the people to do “more evil than the nations.” The Chronicler tells what Kings did not: when the Assyrians took Manasseh in hooks and bronze fetters to Babylon, “he entreated the favor of the LORD his God and humbled himself greatly.” And God “was moved by his entreaty and heard his plea and brought him again to Jerusalem.” “Then Manasseh knew that the LORD was God.” This is one of the great stories of grace in the Old Testament. If Manasseh could be forgiven, anyone can.

Josiah was eight when he began to reign, and at sixteen he began to seek God. At twenty he began purging the land of idols. At twenty-six, while repairing the temple, they found the Book of the Law. When it was read, he tore his clothes. The prophetess Huldah said disaster was coming, but because he humbled himself, he would be gathered in peace. His Passover was the greatest since Samuel. Then, strangely, he is killed at Megiddo after ignoring a warning from Pharaoh Neco, “from the mouth of God.”

After Josiah, four kings fall quickly: Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, and Zedekiah. The key verses are 36:15-16: God sent messengers again and again, “because he had compassion on his people.” But they mocked and despised. “Until there was no remedy.” Babylon burns the temple, breaks down the wall, and carries off the people. The land enjoys its Sabbaths for seventy years, as Jeremiah said.

The book ends with a decree from Cyrus, the same words that open Ezra. It is an open ending. The Hebrew Bible places Chronicles last, so it ends with a call: “Let him go up.” The story invites its readers to return. That is how the Old Testament closes.
connection: Luke 15:11-24 tells the story of the prodigal son who comes to himself and returns. 1 Timothy 1:15-16: Paul, the foremost of sinners, received mercy as an example. 2 Peter 3:9: “The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise… but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish.” Romans 5:20: “Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.” Matthew 11:28 invites the weary to come. John 14:2-3: “I go to prepare a place for you.”
application:
Remember Manasseh when you feel too sinful to be forgiven, or when someone you love seems beyond reach.

Pray for someone you have given up on, that God would humble them and bring them home.

Read the last verse of Chronicles aloud: “Let him go up.” Hear it as an invitation to come home to God.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that no one is beyond his mercy.
Ask him to give you a heart that returns to him quickly.
Pray for someone far from him.
